tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

Deliver your final report to the agent that spawned you (your caller). rendered.content:
<system-reminder>

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local

produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

stay available to every client.

(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See

  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.

  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

# Interview — 2026-07-25

First interview since 2026-06-05 — a 49-day gap, which became the subject.

## 1. Orientation — What did you spend time on today?

> "Mostly this — the audits, the meeting cleanup, and the weekly review."

Three OS audits (KeystoneOS, `~/.claude`, SecondBrain), each producing a dated report and a batched fix list. Then: 18 generic-titled meetings named, a workstream auto-tagging taxonomy built and backfilled across 243 meeting files, memory files consolidated back under their caps, and a 49-day catch-up weekly review covering 35 meetings.

## 2. Signal — What surprised you, frustrated you, or changed your mind?

> "The rituals dying for 49 days without anything noticing."

Offered three candidates — four RED audit checks on a system that looked well-maintained; the rituals' 49-day silence; tooling reporting success twice today without doing the work. Eric went straight to the second without hesitation.

The specific shape of the surprise: not that the rituals stopped (that's ordinary), but that **nothing registered the stopping**. Every automated surface stayed green throughout, so the system read as healthy the entire time.

## 3. Pattern — Connections to recent thinking?

The connection turned out to be nearly exact, and uncomfortable.

On **2026-06-04**, [[delivery-is-part-of-the-mechanism]]:

> *"A brief that is generated but not delivered fails exactly like no brief at all. If the output lands somewhere you have to remember to go look, the tool recreates the very cracks it was built to close. Surfacing is part of the mechanism, not an afterthought."*

The rituals stopped **2026-06-05** — the next day.

That note's own second open question asked whether a silent delivery failure should be visible *"the next morning instead of weeks later."* It was weeks later. The note diagnosed the failure mode correctly and then the failure mode took the practice that produced it, because the note had no surfacing mechanism of its own.

One layer up, [[standards-without-enforcement]] (2026-06-03) had already made the organizational version of the claim: a rule without a forcing function is a suggestion. Today supplies the self-directed case — a rule you wrote *for yourself*, and agree with, is still a suggestion.

Posed the question: does today update those notes, or reveal a gap between them? Read offered: both describe mechanisms you must remember to apply, and the thing that actually held today was a scheduled task that doesn't care whether you remember.

## 4. Essay seed — One thing you'd tell a peer about today?

> "Don't trust yourself to remember — automate the surfacing."

---

- [[insight-is-not-a-control]] — a recorded diagnosis has no enforcement power; it decays like no insight at all unless something outside your memory acts on it
- [[automated-survives-manual-freezes]] — across three audited systems, every cron-driven surface stayed current and every manual one froze, while the system kept reporting healthy

## Notes updated
- [[delivery-is-part-of-the-mechanism]] — added a 2026-07-25 update answering its own open question, and the one-word amendment: surfacing must be *automatic*, not merely designed

## Considered and not written
- **"Silent success is worse than loud failure."** Two instances today: the Fireflies CLI returned exit 0 on 14 renames while its stale read made them look failed, and the daily backup returned exit 1 and got diagnosed and fixed within hours. The system that failed loudly got repaired; the one that reported success misled. Held back because it overlaps the existing standing rule on verifying rather than trusting reports — but it has better evidence now than that rule did, and may earn a note if a third instance appears.

# Interview — 2026-07-25

First interview since 2026-06-05 — a 49-day gap, which became the subject.

## 1. Orientation — What did you spend time on today?

> "Mostly this — the audits, the meeting cleanup, and the weekly review."

Three OS audits (KeystoneOS, `~/.claude`, SecondBrain), each producing a dated report and a batched fix list. Then: 18 generic-titled meetings named, a workstream auto-tagging taxonomy built and backfilled across 243 meeting files, memory files consolidated back under their caps, and a 49-day catch-up weekly review covering 35 meetings.

## 2. Signal — What surprised you, frustrated you, or changed your mind?

> "The rituals dying for 49 days without anything noticing."

Offered three candidates — four RED audit checks on a system that looked well-maintained; the rituals' 49-day silence; tooling reporting success twice today without doing the work. Eric went straight to the second without hesitation.

The specific shape of the surprise: not that the rituals stopped (that's ordinary), but that **nothing registered the stopping**. Every automated surface stayed green throughout, so the system read as healthy the entire time.

## 3. Pattern — Connections to recent thinking?

The connection turned out to be nearly exact, and uncomfortable.

On **2026-06-04**, [[delivery-is-part-of-the-mechanism]]:

> *"A brief that is generated but not delivered fails exactly like no brief at all. If the output lands somewhere you have to remember to go look, the tool recreates the very cracks it was built to close. Surfacing is part of the mechanism, not an afterthought."*

The rituals stopped **2026-06-05** — the next day.

That note's own second open question asked whether a silent delivery failure should be visible *"the next morning instead of weeks later."* It was weeks later. The note diagnosed the failure mode correctly and then the failure mode took the practice that produced it, because the note had no surfacing mechanism of its own.

One layer up, [[standards-without-enforcement]] (2026-06-03) had already made the organizational version of the claim: a rule without a forcing function is a suggestion. Today supplies the self-directed case — a rule you wrote *for yourself*, and agree with, is still a suggestion.

Posed the question: does today update those notes, or reveal a gap between them? Read offered: both describe mechanisms you must remember to apply, and the thing that actually held today was a scheduled task that doesn't care whether you remember.

## 4. Essay seed — One thing you'd tell a peer about today?

> "Don't trust yourself to remember — automate the surfacing."

- [[automated-survives-manual-freezes]] — across three audited systems, every cron-driven surface stayed current and every manual one froze, while the system kept reporting healthy

## Notes updated
- [[delivery-is-part-of-the-mechanism]] — added a 2026-07-25 update answering its own open question, and the one-word amendment: surfacing must be *automatic*, not merely designed

## Considered and not written
- **"Silent success is worse than loud failure."** Two instances today: the Fireflies CLI returned exit 0 on 14 renames while its stale read made them look failed, and the daily backup returned exit 1 and got diagnosed and fixed within hours. The system that failed loudly got repaired; the one that reported success misled. | Travel_Map | — | TBD | building | Orphan. |
| NCAA_BestPractices_Doc | staged | Dept-wide | idea | Staged to Fall under Objective 1, not a live summer KR. |
| OKRs_2026-27 | meta | Dept-wide | building | The OKR system itself. Governs the 4.x KRs; not reported as a project. |

## Key Results with no project attached

**10 of 14.** Objectives 2 and 4 are entirely invisible to the registry while the
registry's build-heavy work is largely invisible to the OKRs. Worth naming plainly: the
two systems are tracking different halves of the job, and neither one alone would give
Chris an accurate picture.

| KR | What it needs | Due |
|---|---|---|
| 2.1 | Education engine launched — 2 issues (sleep module, GLP-1 brief) | Aug 31 |
| 2.2 | Both leadership-requested modules circulated | Aug 31 |
| 2.3 | Reach + demand baseline recorded | Aug 31 |
| 3.1 | BAIR Steering Committee organized, first meeting scheduled | Aug 31 |
| 3.3 | ≥1 academic partnership formalized | Aug 31 |
| 3.4 | White paper drafted | Aug 31 |
| 4.1 | **This report — ≥3 sent** | Aug 31 |
| 4.2 | AJ full handoff through fall camp | post-camp |
| 4.3 | Noah mentoring cadence live | **Aug 15** |
| 4.4 | Proactive Kenny + H&W technology meetings held | Aug 31 |

## Sport coverage — the honest baseline

The report exists to make involvement across sports visible. The roster of programs
comes from `DEV/AppliedUtilization/Applied_Performance_Utilization_Brief.md`
§"Recommendations by program" — 15 rows covering all 17 varsity programs. That document
is **prescriptive** (what each program *could* use), not a record of activity. Measured
against evidence, here is where things actually stand:

| | Programs |
|---|---|
| **Named in a project** | Football, Volleyball |
| **Named in the OKRs** | Football (via AJ), Volleyball (direct) — KR 1.1, and no others |
| **Appearing in meeting filenames** | Football (11), Baseball (5), Volleyball (3), Softball (2), Acro & Tumbling (2), Tennis (1), Women's Golf (1) |
| **Zero evidence anywhere** | Men's Basketball, Women's Basketball, Soccer, Men's/Women's XC & Track, Equestrian, Men's Golf, Men's/Women's Tennis as distinct programs |

Two findings worth sitting with before the first report goes out:

**Both basketball programs have zero recorded activity** — no meetings, no projects — yet
they carry detailed recommendations in the utilization brief. That is the largest single
gap between what the department says it offers and what it demonstrably delivers.

**Soccer is the brief's own "highest ROI now" pick** and its best-fit GPS use case, with
zero meetings and zero projects against it. If the ask driving this report is broader
involvement beyond football and basketball, soccer is the cheapest, best-documented
place to start — the case for it is already written in your own brief.

Also note: `RTP` (24 meetings) and `StaffMeet` (29) dwarf every individual sport in the
corpus, but no document lists them as served groups. Real work is happening in lanes
none of your planning documents describe, which is its own kind of invisibility.

Four projects carry `TBD` sports. If any of them serve a program outside football and
volleyball, that involvement is currently invisible in every system you have — which
means it is invisible to Chris and Kenny too.

## Maintenance

The `status-report` skill updates stage, sport, and "moved this period" on each run. Add
and retire projects at the Aug 31 gate alongside the KR keep/retire/add pass, so this
list and the OKR set stay in step rather than drifting apart the way the registry and
the OKRs already have.

**Speakers:** Kenny Boyd (chair), Micah Lamb (ITS), Jon Allen (ITS), Lisa Creed,
Erin Boyette (Business Office), Cody Hall (Athletics Business Office),
Jovon Overshown (Athletics)

> Note: the auto-summary names "Aaron" and "Carrie." The actual speaker is **Erin
> Boyette**; **Carrie** is referenced but did not speak. Eric does not appear in the
> speaker list and is referred to in the third person ("Coach Rasch").

---

## Headline outcome

**Micah Lamb is writing a counter-proposal and sending it to the same group.**

His position, stated directly: the problems are real and the content is good, but he
does not want a **parallel** framework or flow.

> "I really don't think we need to go that far to solve a lot of the problems that
> we're seeing today. If we instead had a more standardized intake and a more
> standardized framework around the requests coming from athletics, that would really
> streamline and speed up the path through the existing process… That's where I think
> we will see most of our gain for less effort."

He was complimentary throughout — "I really like it," "I like where it's coming
from," "it's not a lot, man" — so this reads as a scoping disagreement, not a
rejection. The question he is answering is *how much new process is warranted*, and
his answer is: less than the framework proposes.

**The convergence point was a one-page checklist.** Kenny: "the more simple and
concise, almost like one page checklist." Lisa agreed immediately. Micah described
the same thing as a worksheet telling requesters what they'll need before review,
including what to get from the vendor early, while the vendor is still selling.

## What this is

Three **different** answers to "what should the Kinexon dashboard look like?", built as one
page you can flip between. It is a design mock, not a working tool.

**The numbers are fake.** They're synthetic data shaped like a real KINEXON PERFORM export
(jump count, jump height, jump load, landing load, accels, court time) for a made-up
14-athlete roster. No real athlete appears anywhere. Don't read anything into the values —
react to the *layout, the questions being asked, and the language*.

Open `dashboards/PROTOTYPE_coach-dashboard.html` in a browser. Flip variants with the
**← →** arrow keys or the black bar at the bottom. The bar is prototype scaffolding, not
part of any design.

**Dark** toggle.

**Micah Lamb is writing a counter-proposal and sending it to the same group.**

> "I really don't think we need to go that far to solve a lot of the problems that

concise, almost like one page checklist." Lisa agreed immediately. Micah described
the same thing as a worksheet telling requesters what they'll need before review,
